note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — INTRODUCED JAPANESE BROME
tiles.details: Follow a complete panicle, not an isolated hanging spikelet. FNA describes an open 10–22 cm panicle with slender flexuous branches and mature spikelets often 20–40 mm with about 6–12 florets; other treatments report shorter 12–20 mm spikelets. These ranges overlap other bromes. Panels 0–2 show real Japanese brome reproductive material, but no current image alone establishes a Central Texas voucher or all key dimensions. A newly locally archived real Texas flowering-grassland photograph from Goldthwaite (panel 11, Sam Kieschnick CC BY) now adds field habit in its actual growing environment. The surrounding grass community is mixed, and the buried roots and exact complete crown-to-head physical connection are NOT shown; do not identify Japanese brome from green growth alone.
tiles.short: Annual with loose often nodding, kinked branches and awned, MULTIFLORED spikelets; confirm glume veins before removal.
tiles.status: REAL TEXAS FIELD HABIT AND MATURE SPIKELETS PHOTOGRAPHED; EXTRACTED CONNECTED ROOT-TO-PANICLE PLANT STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED ANNUAL, SHEATH AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Stefan.lefnaer's CC BY-SA 4.0 source-labelled Austrian original photos are now archived LOCALLY: panel 8 shows true red-brown nodes on hairy green culms with a real 5-mm scale; panel 9 documents hairy leaf sheaths and blade overlap. These pictures show the actual external tissues, not the short INSIDE free 1–2.2 mm membranous ligule. Roots are not exposed. Do not confuse a stem joint, sheath hair, or outer collar with a ligule. Next needed photograph: gently opened same-plant blade/sheath junction face-on with physical millimeter scale, plus continuous connected root-to-panicle evidence. Two more locally stored research-grade species-specific Texas photos now show the actual leaf/sheath exterior held in Rockdale (panel 12) and the lower blade insertion from Mills County (panel 13), both by Linda Jo Conn under individual CC BY licenses. They show exactly WHERE to look for the ligule on a true Japanese brome plant, not the verified 1–2 mm free INNER membranous flap. Panel 11 adds a grassland flowering growth context, but fibrous roots are still buried.
tiles.short: Actual hairy culm nodes/sheaths pictured; true ligule and rooted crown missing
tiles.status: FOUR LOCAL TRUE HAIRY SHEATH/LEAF-COLLAR MACROS INCLUDING TWO TEXAS; FREE LIGULE EDGE AND CONNECTED ROOTS NOT CERTIFIED

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS AND GLUME VEINS
tiles.details: At 10–20× backlight TWO persistent glumes at the BASE of a mature spikelet; do not count lemma veins as glume veins. FNA gives lower glume 4.5–7 mm, upper 5–8 mm, both awnless. Native Texas brome generally has ONE-veined lower and THREE-veined upper glume. Use three authenticated mature spikelets and 1-mm scale before making a confident invasive-versus-native distinction. NEW panel 10 NOW shows an authentic species-specific PAIR OF OUTER GLUMES from the BASE of Japanese brome spikelets, archived from Stefan.lefnaer's actual Austrian specimens (CC BY-SA 4.0). This is significant new photographic evidence for locating true glumes, but the two glume vein counts have NOT been independently resolved from these compressed pixels. Do not add veins or assume (3)5/7 by reading the nearby lemma photo. A calibrated backlit isolated pair remains a hold before removing plants mistaken for native Texas brome.
tiles.short: Usually 6–12 florets; lower glume commonly (3)5-veined, upper usually 7-veined.
tiles.status: ACTUAL BASAL GLUME PAIR NOW PHOTOGRAPHED — LOWER / UPPER NERVE COUNTS NOT YET CERTIFIED

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA BODY, SUBAPICAL AWN AND DRYING TWIST
tiles.details: The lemma is the bract around EACH floret, not an outer glume. FNA describes 7–9 mm lemma bodies, usually 8–13 mm awns arising at least about 1.5 mm below a shallowly bifid apex; awns often diverge or twist as they dry. Existing archived macro shows real lemma and awn outlines but is not a calibrated proof of insertion depth or the vein count. Preserve treatment differences in awn lengths and lemma tip descriptions.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma about 7–9 mm; its one awn usually 8–13 mm and arises below the lemma tip.
tiles.status: REAL MACRO PRESENT — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED AWN INSERTION

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES — DON'T REMOVE TEXAS BROME
tiles.details: Comparison panel 3 is NATIVE Texas brome and is NOT a Japanese brome anatomy photo. Panel 4 is introduced lanceolate brome, often with much longer 25–50 mm spikelets and 8–20 florets. Panel 5 shows native woodland perennial B. pubescens, which can also have a 1/3-veined glume pair. Rescuegrass in panels 6–7 is a DIFFERENT species with broader flattened spikelets. Require actual glume venation, annual roots and lemma anatomy; never decide invasive removal by drooping heads alone.
tiles.short: Native Texas brome has typically 1/3-veined glumes; Japanese brome generally (3)5/7.
tiles.status: NATIVE TEXAS BROME LOOK-ALIKE ARROWS SYNCHRONIZED; NEW JAPANESE GLUME-BASE IMAGE NOT CROSS-SPECIES SUBSTITUTE

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — DIAGNOSTIC MACROS
tiles.details: CANONICAL OCTOBER 27 REAL JAPANESE BROME PHOTOS: ten species-specific archived JPEG records, of which NINE have individually validated openly reusable licenses and appear in the Learner (three older actual mature spikelet/lemma photos, two new Austrian true hairy sheath/culm-node macros, an Austrian true basal-glume photograph, one actual Goldthwaite Texas plant in grassland, one Rockdale external sheath, and one Mills County external blade/collar junction). The tenth, older CC BY-NC iNaturalist image remains an archival research photo, NOT in the public teaching gallery. Fourteen gallery panels total = NINE real Japanese brome photo panels and FIVE OTHER species lookalike panels, two of them still externally served rescuegrass. All six new source images in this pass were physically archived and linked locally, with source creator/photo licenses and image hashes; new images did not receive unsupported anatomical arrows. The native Texas brome comparison uses its corrected canonical markers. ESTIMATED photographic role completeness ~67% (4/6 six-role equivalent): clear reproductive lemma/awn, glume BASE visible but independent vein counts unmeasured, true hairy sheath photographs and outside collar, in-ground Texas live habit with hidden roots, comparisons, and source-labelled panicle recognition. Not fully public-ready: true face-on free 1–2.2 mm ligule, pulled connected fibrous crown-to-head specimen, and individually counted backlit Japanese (3)5/7 versus native Texas 1/3 glume nerves with real 1-mm ruler are missing. Live GitHub Pages deployment and mobile arrows remain unchecked. No extra invasive-removal proof is inferred from head shape.
tiles.short: Nine openly licensed Japanese brome species photos in teaching panels; roots, inside ligule and backlit glume nerves remain.
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 9 PUBLIC-LICENSED TARGET PHOTO PANELS; REAL ROOTS/LIGULE/GLUME NERVES AND PAGES QA REMAIN

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: INTRODUCED JAPANESE BROME: follow slender sometimes KINKED, arching panicle branches bearing several hanging AWNED MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets. At 10–20× count glume veins: lower commonly 3–5, upper often 7 (FNA); compare rare native Texas brome lower ONE and upper THREE. The awns on Japanese's individual lemmas can be twisted/divergent. Panicle droop and awn color alone never prove ID.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with the annotated ORIGINAL real photo. Follow a FLOWERING PANICLE branch to one MULTI-FLOWERED SPIKELET; each overlapping scale is a distinct lemma/floret, not one giant grain.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Stefan.lefnaer's CC BY-SA 4.0 source-labelled Austrian original photos are now archived LOCALLY: panel 8 shows true red-brown nodes on hairy green culms with a real 5-mm scale; panel 9 documents hairy leaf sheaths and blade overlap. These pictures show the actual external tissues, not the short INSIDE free 1–2.2 mm membranous ligule. Roots are not exposed. Do not confuse a stem joint, sheath hair, or outer collar with a ligule. Next needed photograph: gently opened same-plant blade/sheath junction face-on with physical millimeter scale, plus continuous connected root-to-panicle evidence. Two more locally stored research-grade species-specific Texas photos now show the actual leaf/sheath exterior held in Rockdale (panel 12) and the lower blade insertion from Mills County (panel 13), both by Linda Jo Conn under individual CC BY licenses. They show exactly WHERE to look for the ligule on a true Japanese brome plant, not the verified 1–2 mm free INNER membranous flap. Panel 11 adds a grassland flowering growth context, but fibrous roots are still buried.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: At 10–20× backlight TWO persistent glumes at the BASE of a mature spikelet; do not count lemma veins as glume veins. FNA gives lower glume 4.5–7 mm, upper 5–8 mm, both awnless. Native Texas brome generally has ONE-veined lower and THREE-veined upper glume. Use three authenticated mature spikelets and 1-mm scale before making a confident invasive-versus-native distinction. NEW panel 10 NOW shows an authentic species-specific PAIR OF OUTER GLUMES from the BASE of Japanese brome spikelets, archived from Stefan.lefnaer's actual Austrian specimens (CC BY-SA 4.0). This is significant new photographic evidence for locating true glumes, but the two glume vein counts have NOT been independently resolved from these compressed pixels. Do not add veins or assume (3)5/7 by reading the nearby lemma photo. A calibrated backlit isolated pair remains a hold before removing plants mistaken for native Texas brome.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: Stefan.lefnaer's Austrian microscope photograph shows broad green lemma bodies with pale margins and long slender attached awns. The 5-mm source scale is visible below. These are LEMMAS, not the two outer glumes. This view does not expose the true ligule, separate the two glumes for vein counting, or establish a Texas voucher.

panels.label: JAPANESE BROME — visible nervation, overlapping lemmas, awn origins
panels.caption: Look at the folded overlapping florets and the fine awns projecting from near, but slightly below, each lemma apex. The branching grassy head and glume pairs are OFF FRAME: this close-up teaches florets and awn attachment only, not exact glume nerve counts or Hays County provenance.

panels.label: REAL CULM NODES — reddish joints and hairy external sheaths with source scale
panels.caption: Stefan.lefnaer's four source-identified Japanese brome stem views show dark/purple true culm nodes, adjacent green internodes and many long fine external sheath hairs. The photographer's 5-mm bar offers a genuine reference; do not confuse a culm NODE with the INTERNAL free ligule at a blade–sheath seam. This original Austrian stem is not a Texas voucher, and roots are out of frame.

panels.label: TRUE HAIRY LEAF SHEATH — actual blade–sheath overlap (inner ligule hidden)
panels.caption: Real Japanese brome vegetative anatomy from the Austrian source-labelled specimen: green leaf blade and hairy external sheath are photographed with a printed 5-mm scale. The inner free membrane itself has not been pulled open face-on; the long outer hairs should NOT be labeled as a diagnostic ligule. Distinguish a leaf-sheath junction from a true culm node.

The thin outer bracts are GLUMES, not the overlapping many-floret lemmas. This closes the previous 'no glume image' gap, but counting the (3)5 versus 7 dorsal glume veins from these combined original views still requires pixel/microscope verification and should not be illustrated by invented vein arrows.

intro: INTRODUCED JAPANESE BROME: follow slender sometimes KINKED, arching panicle branches bearing several hanging AWNED MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets. At 10–20× count glume veins: lower commonly 3–5, upper often 7 (FNA); compare rare native Texas brome lower ONE and upper THREE. The awns on Japanese's individual lemmas can be twisted/divergent. Panicle droop and awn color alone never prove ID.
memory_rule: JAPANESE: annual, flexuous awned head, higher glume veins. TEXAS: annual, lower ONE & upper THREE glume veins. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spikelets. WOODLAND: perennial + hairy lemmas. RESCUE: broad flat short/no-awn units (comparison only).
safety_note: Four exact-species JPEG records are physically archived in GitHub; three of the ten comparison panels (0–2) display archived Japanese brome, panels 3–7 show other bromes/rescuegrass, and panels 8–9 externally reference source-verified hairy nodes/sheaths (not a true ligule). Stefan.lefnaer's archived lemma/awn photo contains a genuine 5-mm scale and existing visible-structure arrows, but isolated glume vein counts, inner ligule, precise awn insertion, and a rooted Central Texas voucher are still missing. Preserve individual CC BY-NC / CC BY-SA rights and attribution. FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS; live site NOT VERIFIED.
field_rule: For native versus introduced Bromus, the important structures are glume VEINS, actual lemma dimensions and awns, and an annual or perennial rooted crown—not the word 'brome' or a pretty nodding head.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
